projects.name: IterViz
projects.tagline: Visual AI agent orchestrator that turns a sentence into a system architecture and working code.
projects.summary: A full-stack app where you describe a software idea in plain English, an LLM Architect generates a graph-based system contract, and a multi-agent Orchestrator implements each component in real time. A React Flow frontend lets you explore the contract, inspect per-node implementation subgraphs, and watch agents work over WebSocket.
details: IterViz targets the handoff from a vague idea to running code. The backend is built with FastAPI and uses Pydantic schemas as a single source of truth across the entire pipeline.

Phase 1 — Planning: the Architect agent reads a natural-language prompt and produces a Contract (nodes for services, stores, UI, and external APIs; edges for data, control, and event flow). A Compiler agent then audits the contract for structural invariants and asks the user clarifying questions before the design is frozen.

Phase 2 — Implementation: the Orchestrator dispatches subagents, tracks assignments through drafted → in_progress → implemented, and finally runs a Connector pass to wire the generated modules into a runnable main.py.
The frontend is a React + TypeScript + Tailwind app using React Flow for the architecture graph and Zustand for contract, subgraph, and WebSocket state. Progress is streamed live to the browser.

I built the backend agents, the contract compiler/verifier, the orchestration engine, the REST and WebSocket APIs, and the frontend graph visualization components. The project is end-to-end functional and includes pytest coverage for chunking, pipeline orchestration, and storage adapter behavior.

projects.name: Brawl Stars Draft Board
projects.tagline: Interactive Brawl Stars draft board with drag-and-drop brawler categorization.
projects.summary: A web tool inspired by pro-tier brawler role maps. Organize brawlers into adjustable role columns, attach multiple ability tags to each bubble, and save or load draft boards as plain JSON.
details: The app seeds a default board from a reference role map and lets the user fully customize columns and tags.

Each brawler is a draggable bubble. Bubbles can be moved between columns, renamed, or deleted. Tags are managed through a separate key panel with name and color editing, and each brawler can carry any number of tags.
State is persisted to a folder of your choice as brawlers.json and config.json, making drafts portable and version-controllable.
I wrote the Flask backend, the vanilla-JS drag-and-drop logic, the tag and column editor, and the persistence layer. It is a small but complete single-page app.

projects.name: Flow Matching Learning
projects.tagline: Turn lecture PDFs, slides, and videos into an interactive concept graph.
projects.summary: A hackathon-style pipeline that ingests course materials, transcribes media, extracts text and diagrams from PDFs, embeds chunks, and uses an LLM reasoning chain to build a navigable knowledge graph of concepts and prerequisite links.
details: Phase A ingestion runs on Modal serverless GPUs: Whisper for audio and video transcription, a VLM for PDF and slide text and image extraction, and an embedding service for chunk vectorization. Results are stored in Actian VectorAI for similarity search.

Phase B reasoning uses OpenAI to: (1) generate a hierarchical table of contents from the material, (2) extract key concepts for each section, and (3) validate prerequisite and related edges between concepts using vector similarity and LLM judgment.
The backend exposes FastAPI endpoints and an end-to-end CLI, while the frontend renders the resulting graph_data.json as an interactive React Flow graph.

I designed the multi-stage pipeline, the compute-boundary enforcement layer, the versioned prompt templates, the hyperparameter config, and the frontend graph consumer. The system works end-to-end on sample data but still needs quality and robustness improvements.

projects.name: SAI Soccer RL
projects.tagline: Reinforcement learning for humanoid robot soccer in the SAI Booster Soccer Showdown.
projects.summary: An exploration into training soccer-playing policies for the Booster T1 humanoid robot. Includes MuJoCo teleoperation, motion mimicry, imitation-learning baselines, and DDPG/SAC training scripts.
details: The environment is the SAI Booster Soccer Showdown, a MuJoCo-based competition focused on generalizable robot soccer. I set up a local teleoperation harness that maps keyboard commands to SE3 joystick-style control of the lower-body robot.

The mimic/ tools compute forward kinematics and replay reference motion files to understand robot state and action structure. The imitation_learning/ directory contains JAX/Flax implementations of behavior cloning (BC), IQL, GCIQL, and HIQL agents, plus replay buffers and Weights & Biases logging.
I also wrote DDPG and SAC training loops, observation preprocessors that concatenate robot state, ball state, and environment info, and model checkpoints for submission to the SAI benchmark.
This repo is a work in progress: the training pipeline runs but the learned policies do not yet achieve reliable soccer behavior, and the SAI client integration still needs finishing.

projects.name: QuantConnect Crypto
projects.tagline: Experimental machine-learning crypto trading bot on QuantConnect.
projects.summary: A QuantConnect algorithm that computes a basket of technical indicators each hour and feeds rolling-window features into a scikit-learn model to decide long/short/hold positions on BTC/USDT.
details: The algorithm ingests hourly Binance market data and computes indicators including MACD, VWAP, RSI, ADX, CCI, Stochastic, CMO, and Ultimate Oscillator.

For each symbol, it maintains rolling windows of recent indicator values and passes them to a persisted scikit-learn model loaded from the QuantConnect object store. The model outputs one of three signals: short, hold, or long.
Position sizing is controlled by a fixed-invest fraction, with profit-taking at a 5% gain and a stop-loss at a 5% loss. A cooldown period prevents rapid trading.
This was an early exploration into algorithmic trading; most backtests lost money, so the project is archived as a learning exercise rather than a working strategy.
